content: 1. A national One Health investment portfolio should include a package of prioritized investment opportunities to guide resource allocation effectively. 2. Mechanisms must be established to ensure that funding is directed toward or leveraged for prioritized activities. This may require specialized negotiations, financial agreements, or in-kind mechanisms to secure the necessary resources. 3. The results of the implementation plan should be communicated clearly to demonstrate the effective use of resources, highlight successes, and share lessons learned. 4. Resource mobilization activities should be monitored continuously to refine and optimize efforts as needed. 5. Once a national One Health investment strategy with a clear set of prioritized opportunities is developed, it should be treated as an active plan managed by a dedicated task team. This team should include individuals capable of championing and advocating for the strategy at both national and international levels. 6. The task team should actively identify and engage potential partners through advocacy efforts to raise awareness of investment opportunities, understand the priorities of partners and investors, and work collaboratively to identify synergies. 7. The Quadripartite (FAO, UNEP, WHO, and WOAH) can assist in matching countries’ needs with available funding resources and provide evidence for cost-effectiveness studies on One Health actions. 8. A monitoring, evaluation, and learning (MEL) framework should be developed and adapted at the national level. This framework is essential to ensure that projects and programs achieve their objectives through measurable outputs, outcomes, and impacts. 9. The MEL framework should also identify and address challenges impeding progress and allow for the realignment of programs and activities as necessary. Monitoring focuses on inputs, activities, outputs, and short-term outcomes, while evaluation emphasizes longer-term outcomes and impacts. 10. The learning component of MEL is critical, as it derives valuable knowledge from lessons learned during development interventions. This includes the ability to analyze and use data effectively at both national and subnational levels for decision-making, planning, programming, and implementation. 11. Baseline indicators should be developed based on assessments related to One Health. Key performance indicators for MEL should align with the three pathways of the theory of change and be monitored against existing MEL frameworks for various technical programs and action tracks within the One Health Joint Plan of Action (OH JPA). 12. Indicators should be incorporated into the national One Health action plan and reflect principles such as equity, inclusion, balance, stewardship, and transdisciplinarity. Definitions, funding sources, timeframes, and sustainability measures should be integrated into the MEL frameworks. 13. A holistic measure of outcomes, including trade-offs, co-benefits, added value, and risk mitigation strategies identified through a One Health approach, should be captured throughout the MEL processes. These considerations are expected to become more robust as equitable processes evolve and relevant stakeholders are included. 14. Benchmarks should be defined, and progress should be monitored against these benchmarks to provide concrete evidence of achievements, support advocacy efforts, and stimulate further progress. 15. Effective implementation of the One Health approach often yields long-term outcomes, which should be included in MEL frameworks and linked to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 16. A periodic feedback mechanism for data and evidence from One Health implementation and research should be established to inform policy and program adoption continuously. Both primary and secondary data sources should be utilized throughout the implementation phase. 17. A process evaluation system should be built to guide the implementation of the OH JPA effectively. The Quadripartite is currently developing a MEL framework with targets and indicators to measure and facilitate reporting on OH JPA progress. 18. The targets of the OH JPA should be linked to their contributions toward achieving relevant SDG targets. MEL should also be used to periodically revise the implementation guide for the OH JPA to adapt to changing priorities, conditions, and goals. 19. The implementation of national One Health action plans involves executing activities at the national level according to the plans. Ideally, countries will have followed the recommended preparatory steps and be ready to implement their new or adapted activities. 20. Identified gaps should have been addressed or be in the process of being addressed based on prioritization exercises conducted during the planning phase, considering enablers and barriers to implementation. 21. Implementation activities should focus on the four main pillars of coordination, collaboration, communication, and capacity-building, as outlined in the One Health definition. 22. Technical guidance and resources for each pillar and the six action tracks of the OH JPA should be identified and consulted to support the implementation of national action plan activities. 23. Stakeholders identified during the planning phase should now be mobilized and engaged in implementation according to their mandates and expertise. 24. Support from Quadripartite organizations and other relevant development partners should be identified, and sustainability issues should be discussed. 25. A situation analysis should have been completed, and a national multisectoral One Health coordination mechanism should have been established or adapted. 26. A national One Health action plan with prioritized activities and responsible stakeholder groups should have been developed. This plan should link OH JPA action tracks to the three pathways of change and align with existing relevant national action plans, frameworks, and strategies. 27. National One Health action plans should be institutionalized by the respective ministries to ensure sustainable and reliable implementation, follow-up, and MEL. 28. MEL should be ongoing throughout the implementation of activities, and countries should refer to their MEL frameworks to provide feedback and evaluate outputs and data from all implementation steps. 29. Countries may prepare annual reports on One Health implementation, led by their multisectoral One Health coordination mechanisms. These reports should ideally be shared through regular exchanges, knowledge platforms, international conferences, regional networks, and symposia. 30. National One Health plans should be reviewed, aligned, and adapted to the global OH JPA to collectively achieve the six key objectives. Adequate guidance and tools should be provided for the effective implementation of One Health approaches to promote the health of humans, animals, plants, and ecosystems and to prevent and manage risks at the human-animal-plant-environment interface. 31. Efforts should aim to reduce the risk and minimize the local and global impacts of zoonotic epidemics and pandemics by understanding the linkages and drivers of emergence and spillover, adopting upstream prevention, and strengthening One Health surveillance, early warning, and response systems. 32. The burden of endemic zoonotic, neglected tropical, and vector-borne diseases should be reduced by supporting countries in implementing community-centric, risk-based solutions, strengthening policy and legal frameworks across sectors, and increasing political commitment and investment. 33. Awareness, policy changes, and action coordination among stakeholders should be promoted to ensure that humans, animals, and ecosystems achieve and maintain health in their interactions along the food supply chain. 34. Joint action should be taken to preserve antimicrobial efficacy and ensure sustainable and equitable access to antimicrobials for responsible and prudent use in human, animal, and plant health.
